CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 127 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/31/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 4




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                           )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                             ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                           )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                            )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                               )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                                  )


                     Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of Jason J. Thenmadathil

         Direct Testimony

                In his Direct Testimony, Jason Thenmadathil first provides his educational qualifications
         and employment history. He is Director of Regulatory Accounting for Oklahoma Gas and Electric
         Company. The overall purpose of his testimony is to present the results of an analysis undertaken
         by OG&E, utilizing the most recently approved cost of service study, which demonstrates
         downward rate pressure to the existing customer base from the proposed Google data centers. In
         addition, he sponsors the estimated customer impact associated with the two Capacity Purchase
         Agreements being requested for recovery in this case.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil testified that the addition of a large-load data center such as Google can
         provide tangible benefits to existing customers. He explained that these facilities typically operate
         at high load factors, drawing a consistent and predictable level of power, which allows the utility
         to spread its fixed system costs across a much larger volume of sales, creating downward pressure
         on rates. He stated that production demand allocators, which assign the costs of the generation
         fleet to different customer classes based on their contribution to system peaks, would shift
         significantly with the addition of Google’s substantial and steady demand, reducing the
         proportional share of fixed production costs that must be recovered from other customer classes.
         He further testified that all embedded system costs, including operations and maintenance
         expenses, employee salaries, and software related expenditures, will be shared with Google
         through the allocation process, benefiting other customers.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil then testified that the Company modified its most recently approved cost
         of service study from Case No. PUD 2023-000087 to demonstrate how the addition of the Google
         data centers could impact other customers. He explained that this analysis is not meant to represent
         a cost of service study designed for setting new rates, but rather an illustrative study for the purpose
         of presenting a targeted incremental impact analysis that isolates the impact of Google’s load. He
         stated that the analysis demonstrates a shift that reduces costs for existing customers, translating
         into residential customer benefits of approximately $1.83 per month with Google’s load at
               by 2027, growing to an estimated $5.33 per month at                by 2031, and $6.84 per month
         at             by 2036. He testified that even current Large Power and Light customers experience
         a benefit despite the production demand allocator increasing for the entire class, because the
         substantial amount of demand and kilowatt-hours added still results in other members of that class
         seeing a benefit. He further stated that by the time Google reaches approximately                     of

         contract demand, customers would have benefited from about $130 million of cost shifting,
         calculated by taking the total revenue requirement for recently approved and pending generation
         projects from 2027 through 2036 and calculating the total class revenue requirement difference
         between current settled production demand allocators and modified allocators reflecting Google’s
         load.

                  Mr. Thenmadathil testified that the Google contract contains a provision recognizing that
         any potential adverse rate impact to other customer classes resulting from the cost of providing
         service to Google will be reviewed and addressed in each general rate proceeding. He explained
         that this assurance could take the form of a separate cost of service study performed and submitted
         in a future rate case, testing whether Google had an adverse rate impact for other customers by
         comparing a cost of service study with and without Google’s load and a proportional share of their
         contributing generation need. He stated that this provision allows the Commission to review the
         impact and decide how to address any negative impact, giving additional assurance that current
         customers will not be negatively impacted due to changes occurring in the future.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil also testified regarding the customer impact of the Rush Springs and
         High Spring Capacity Purchase Agreements. He stated that OG&E requests rider cost recovery to
         begin once the Commission has approved the projects and the Company begins incurring costs,
         with costs for the Rush Springs CPA included in the FCA rider when OG&E begins paying for
         delivered capacity in 2027 and the High Spring CPA beginning in 2028. He explained that the
         customer impact was calculated using the standard allocation method typically used for pre-
         approval cases, applying the most recently approved production demand allocator from Case No.
         PUD 2023-000087, resulting in a monthly bill impact for residential customers of approximately
         $0.13 per month in 2027, $0.41 per month in 2028, and $0.46 per month in 2029. He testified that
         since the CPAs provided by Google are below-market price, there is a benefit to customers, and
         that selection of the Google CPAs equates to a savings of about $0.60 per month in 2029 when
         compared to the least cost CPA executed through the RFP, as discussed in the testimony of OG&E
         witness Schuermann.

         Rebuttal Testimony

                In his Rebuttal Testimony, Mr. Thenmadathil explained the purpose of his testimony is to
         respond to arguments raised in the Responsive Testimony of the Attorney General, Oklahoma
         Sustainability Network, and the Public Utility Division.

                  Mr. Thenmadathil testified that he did not include estimates of future generation resources
         or other potential system investments in his analysis because such estimates are not known and
         measurable at this time. He explained that the Company has not presented future generation
         facilities, the timing of such facilities, or the costs to the Commission for pre-approval, and that
         any attempt to quantify such impacts would be highly speculative. He then testified that the future
         is a two-way street, noting that if future unknown costs should be considered, then future unknown
         benefits must also be recognized. He stated that future transmission investment, distribution
         investment, generation resources, software investment, and other system costs incurred for the
         benefit of all customers may be spread across a larger load base due to the addition of the data

         center, and that those future cost sharing benefits are not reflected in his analysis for the same
         reason future generation costs are not reflected: neither can be reliably quantified today.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil testified that the Electric Service Agreements contain a protective
         provision requiring the Company to study and present the impacts of serving the data center load
         in future rate proceedings, including whether the customer’s service by OG&E is resulting in
         adverse impacts to other customers. He stated that this approach is preferable because it allows
         decisions to be made using actual data rather than assumptions, and that if future costs exceed
         benefits and create adverse rate impacts to other customers, those impacts can be identified and
         addressed in a future rate proceeding. He noted that all parties generally agreed to the concept of
         the adverse impact analysis, and that the AG agreed with the concept but had recommendations on
         how to specifically conduct the analysis. He testified that OG&E would not recommend the
         Commission adopt specific parameters surrounding the study at this time, until actual known and
         measurable data is available to conduct the study, and that the Company will provide the full with
         and without study in a general rate filing which includes Google as a customer, along with all
         workpapers, results, and testimony explaining how the study was conducted.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil then addressed several specific party recommendations. Regarding AG
         witness Beling’s recommendation that allocation factors should be updated more frequently and
         that there be a true-up for Construction Work in Progress, he testified that in Case No. PUD2025-
         000082, OG&E proposed a true-up mechanism and annual allocation update for its requested
         CWIP rider, and that although that tariff was not approved, OG&E intends to recommend a similar
         mechanism in the event it requests CWIP in the future. He also noted that AG witness Beling’s
         arguments about regulatory lag of allocation factors are compelling reasons why the Commission
         should consider adopting some sort of performance-based rate mechanism. Regarding arguments
         by AG witness Beling and OIEC witness Garrett that any future transmission costs associated with
         the Google load should be directly borne by Google, he testified that the treatment of any future
         transmission costs should be addressed in a future proceeding such as the large load tariff case or
         a general rate case, and that with the fail safe mechanism in the contract, customers would not be
         adversely affected from additional transmission costs needed specifically for Google in the with
         and without study. Regarding the PUD’s recommendation on the timing of performing the adverse
         impact analysis, he testified that the Company’s proposed approach of performing the analysis in
         an annual fuel prudency review or a general rate case is more appropriate, because a general rate
         case is the proceeding in which the Company’s revenue requirement, cost allocation
         methodologies, and billing determinants are updated and used to establish customer rates. He
         stated that more frequent review may be appropriate for fuel-related impacts, as fuel costs are
         already subject to periodic review outside of base rate proceedings and are adjusted through
         existing, separate regulatory mechanisms.

                 Mr. Thenmadathil concluded by summarizing that the analysis presented in his Direct
         Testimony focused on known and measurable impacts, that future costs and future benefits are
         both unknown today, and that OG&E has appropriately proposed a with and without evaluation in
         a general rate case using actual costs and benefits for the Commission to evaluate. He further
         noted that the ESAs appropriately address uncertainty through a fail safe provision requiring future
         evaluation of actual system impacts and providing a forum for any adverse effects to be identified
         and addressed using real data.
